title: Resident set capture and threshold search notes
content:
Goal:
Capture a realistic resident set (RSet) of KV pages for our serving workload and search for eviction/occupancy thresholds that minimize paging and downstream CPU stalls while keeping latency SLO

Summary / hypothesis:
- We suspect that our current conservative residency target (retain 90% of hot pages) is over-provisioning GPU/host memory for small-to-medium models and hurting multi-tenant density.
- Hypothesis: a lower target (70–80%) plus an adaptive fast-path for tail requests will reduce memory pressure and overall batch latency variance without materially increasing page faults for typical workloads.

What we measured (instrumentation):
- Kernel level samples: pagemap-based residency dumps taken from the inference process at 10s intervals during 30m run (script: tools/residency/dump-residency.sh).
- Perf counters on host: LLC-misses, mem-load-latency, DRAM-reads (pcm/likwid).
- GPU observable: PCIe reads (nvprof counters), stalled cycles due to page transfer (instrumented in runtime tracing).
- Event traces: combined perf-trace + runtime-span export to jaeger for correlation (trace ids present in dump headers).

Experiment setup:
- Cluster: dev-cluster-5 (A100 80GB nodes, 8 pods per node in this test; test tenant: sandbox-1)
- Model: small-medium transformer (6.7B) with KV cache hotset estimated ~2.1GB per request involving long contexts.
- Traffic: synthetic mix modeled from production traces (60% short chat, 40% long context extraction). QPS: 220 per node.
- Baseline: current residency-policy = ALWAYS_PIN_HOT with target_residency_pct=90
- Candidates: target_residency_pct = [95,90,85,80,75,70]; prefetch window = [0,4,8,16 frames]; eviction grace period = [0s,1s,5s].

Key scripts and commands used:
- Dump residency: tools/residency/dump-residency.sh --pid $PID --out /tmp/residies/$(date +%s).json
- Aggregate perf: tools/perf/aggregate-host.sh --interval 10s --duration 1800s --tags residency-test-v1
- Generate synthetic load: tools/loadgen/mix-replay --trace samples/prod-mix-2025-09.json --qps 220 --seed 42

Representative observations (high level):
1) Residency distributions are highly bimodal across requests: small requests touch a narrow ~200–400MB working set, long-context requests touch a much larger tail.
2) When target_residency_pct <= 80%, we see a modest (1.2–1.8x) increase in page-in events per long request, BUT overall average p50 latency across all requests decreased ~6–9% due to improved packing/throughput on node (fewer pages pinned globally).
3) Tail latencies (p99) for long-context requests increased when target_residency_pct <= 75% by ~18–30%. This was correlated with elevated DRAM read spikes and host CPU cycles spent on page migration.
4) Prefetch window of 8 frames reduced p99 regressions with 75–80% targets, suggesting prefetching amortizes page-in latency for multi-chunk generation. 16 frames gave diminishing returns and introduced excess PCIe traffic for short requests.

Metrics excerpt (aggregated):
- Baseline (90%): mean page-ins/hour/node = 1200; p50 latency = 56 ms; p99 latency = 210 ms; host LLC-miss rate = 12.3%
- 80% target + prefetch=8: mean page-ins/hour/node = 1800; p50 latency = 50 ms; p99 latency = 235 ms; host LLC-miss rate = 13.9%
- 75% target + prefetch=8 + grace=1s: mean page-ins/hour/node = 2500; p50 latency = 48 ms; p99 latency = 260 ms; host LLC-miss rate = 16.7%

Operational notes / surprising findings:
- Page-in cost is not linear with size: bursts of many small page-ins (a few KB each due to fragmentation) caused longer stalls than fewer large transfers. Our allocator fragmentation correlates strongly with page-in latency spikes.
- NUMA locality: page-ins for replicas placed on remote NUMA nodes increased host stalls by ~30% vs local. We must consider binding or migrate-preferred policy for kernel pin actions.
- Persistent tail: a small fraction (~0.7%) of long-context requests consistently triggered the largest page-in storms. These appear to be requests recomputing rarely used tokens (long prompts with many unique prefixes). They dominate p99.

Qualitative trade-offs:
- Density vs tail: Lower residency increases density but shifts cost into tail page-ins and CPU stalls. This will be acceptable for many PLG customers but risky for enterprise customers with strict p99 SLOs.
- Prefetch helps but must be applied selectively: aggressive prefetch increases PCIe/DRAM traffic and hurts short requests if uncontrolled.

Proposed adaptive policy (sketch):
1) Per-request fast classifier: predict if request will be long-context (based on prompt length + heuristic token-entropy) -> classify as SHORT/LONG.
2) SHORT requests: aggressive eviction allowed (target_residency_pct = 65–75), prefetch window = 0.
3) LONG requests: conservative retention (target_residency_pct = 90), prefetch window = 8, grace period = 1s.
4) For multi-tenant nodes: enforce per-tenant soft caps to prevent noisy-neighbor page-in storms; throttle prefetch traffic when DRAM or PCIe counters exceed threshold.

Instrumentation follow-ups (next experiments):
- Repeat with allocator tuning to reduce fragmentation (tcmalloc/hoard knobs) to see if tail page-in storms reduce.
- Run same sweep on smaller GPU (H100 80GB) and cheaper GPUs (A10) to evaluate cross-hardware trade-offs; expected different PCIe behaviors.
- Add per-request cost-accounting spans into traces to attribute CPU-page-in hops to individual request IDs (helps in noisy-neighbor debugging).
- Explore streaming prefetch: prefetch only top-K likely future KV pages (predictive) instead of contiguous windows.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- What default residency target do we ship for Hosted? (team input requested)
- Do we expose per-route residency controls in Console or keep as automated policy? (product question)
- Should Dedicated be allowed to opt into more permissive eviction to maximize density? (sales/enterprise implications)

Immediate action items (owners):
- Aisha: run allocator-fragmentation sweep on dev-cluster-5 and attach diff to this doc (due 2026-03-17).
- Ben: add per-request tracing spans to the runtime and instrument page-in attribution (PR draft: linked above) (due 2026-03-24).
- Miguel: run hardware sweep on H100 and A10 variants and collect perf counters (due 2026-03-31).
- Sofia (me): draft proposal for adaptive residency policy for product review (due 2026-03-21).

Notes to self: keep experiment seeds and raw dumps in gs://redwood-inference-residency/2026-03-10/; large binary files retained for 30 days. Avoid changing the production retention policy until allocator tests complete.
